lessonTitle: Common Overdoses and Antidotes: Paracetamol, Opioids, Benzodiazepines and Salicylates

blocks.text: A young woman takes a large number of paracetamol tablets after an argument and feels well apart from mild nausea. Two days later she is jaundiced with a rising INR. The first day of paracetamol poisoning is deceptively quiet, which is why every overdose needs a plan based on mechanism, timing and antidote.

blocks.markdown: This unit covers three common overdoses and their antidotes: paracetamol (acetaminophen) and acetylcysteine, opioids and benzodiazepines with naloxone and flumazenil, and salicylates (aspirin). Doses and thresholds that appear are teaching examples, not treatment instructions; local protocols and toxicology advice apply.

blocks.title: Paracetamol hepatotoxicity
blocks.text: At therapeutic doses most paracetamol is conjugated to glucuronide and sulfate and excreted. A small fraction is oxidised by cytochrome P450 (mainly CYP2E1) to the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), which is detoxified by conjugation with glutathione. In overdose the conjugation pathways saturate, more NAPQI forms, glutathione is depleted and NAPQI binds covalently to hepatocyte proteins, causing centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis.

blocks.markdown: Clinically, there is an early phase of nausea and vomiting or no symptoms, then right upper quadrant pain and rising transaminases at 24 to 72 hours, then possible liver failure with coagulopathy, encephalopathy and renal injury. **Acetylcysteine** is the antidote: it replenishes glutathione (it is a cysteine donor) and can also bind NAPQI directly. It is most effective when started within about 8 hours of ingestion but is still beneficial later. Decisions rely on the time of ingestion and a plasma paracetamol concentration taken at 4 hours or later, plotted on a treatment nomogram; where the time is unknown or ingestion was staggered, treatment is often given on the basis of risk and liver tests. Risk factors for toxicity at lower doses include chronic alcohol excess, malnutrition and enzyme-inducing drugs.

blocks.title: Estimating the ingested dose
blocks.prompt: A 48 kg woman reports taking 24 tablets of 500 mg paracetamol. Calculate the dose in mg/kg.
blocks.answer: 250 mg/kg, which is a potentially toxic ingestion needing assessment with timed plasma levels and discussion with the toxicology service.

rows: Start early; anaphylactoid reactions can occur with infusion
Short duration; re-sedation; precipitates withdrawal in dependent patients
Competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptors
Can precipitate seizures in dependent patients or with pro-convulsant co-ingestants such as tricyclics
Alkalinise urine with sodium bicarbonate; haemodialysis in severe cases
blocks.caption: Antidotes and cautions.

blocks.markdown: **Opioid overdose** causes the triad of reduced consciousness, small (pinpoint) pupils and respiratory depression. Naloxone reverses it, but its duration (roughly 30 to 90 minutes) is shorter than that of many opioids such as methadone and modified-release preparations, so patients can slip back into respiratory depression and need observation and repeat doses or an infusion. In opioid-dependent patients large doses precipitate acute withdrawal, so titrate small doses to restore adequate breathing. **Benzodiazepine overdose** causes sedation and respiratory depression, usually mild when taken alone; supportive care is usually enough. Flumazenil is restricted to selected cases because it may precipitate seizures, particularly in long-term users or mixed overdoses.

**Salicylate poisoning.** Salicylates directly stimulate the respiratory centre, causing hyperventilation and a respiratory alkalosis, and uncouple oxidative phosphorylation, causing heat production, increased metabolic demand, lactate and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Features: tinnitus and deafness, nausea and vomiting, sweating, hyperventilation, fever, agitation, confusion and in severe cases seizures, coma and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Children often show metabolic acidosis earlier than adults. Treatment includes charcoal for recent ingestion, correction of fluid and potassium, intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise the urine and promote salicylate excretion, and haemodialysis for severe poisoning.

blocks.caption: Concentrations in mmol/L; the reference interval varies by laboratory (roughly 8 to 16 mmol/L without potassium). A raised gap indicates unmeasured acid anions.

blocks.title: Anion gap in a poisoned patient
blocks.prompt: A hyperventilating patient has Na 138, Cl 102 and bicarbonate 14 mmol/L. Calculate the anion gap and interpret it.

steps.text: A gap of 22 is raised, indicating a high anion gap metabolic acidosis as in salicylate poisoning (also seen in lactic acidosis and ketoacidosis).

blocks.answer: Anion gap 22 mmol/L: raised, consistent with unmeasured acid anions.

blocks.title: Antidote pitfalls
blocks.text: Naloxone and flumazenil are shorter-acting than many of the drugs they reverse. Never discharge a patient shortly after reversal, and do not use flumazenil where seizure risk is high.

points: Paracetamol overdose depletes glutathione so NAPQI injures the liver; acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and works best when started early.
Naloxone reverses opioids but is short-acting and may precipitate withdrawal; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines but may precipitate seizures.
Salicylate poisoning causes tinnitus, hyperventilation, respiratory alkalosis with metabolic acidosis, sweating and fever, treated with bicarbonate and dialysis in severe cases.

questions.stem: What is the key event leading to hepatocyte necrosis in paracetamol overdose?

options.text: Depletion of glutathione so that NAPQI accumulates and binds to liver proteins

questions.correctOptionText: Depletion of glutathione so that NAPQI accumulates and binds to liver proteins
questions.explanation: Conjugation pathways saturate and glutathione runs out. NAPQI then binds covalently to hepatocyte proteins, causing centrilobular necrosis.

questions.stem: How does acetylcysteine protect the liver after paracetamol overdose?

options.text: It replenishes glutathione and can bind NAPQI
It blocks absorption in the gut
It induces CYP2E1 to remove paracetamol faster
It dissolves toxic metabolites by alkalinising urine

questions.correctOptionText: It replenishes glutathione and can bind NAPQI

distractorRationale.b: That is the role of charcoal.

questions.explanation: Acetylcysteine supplies cysteine for glutathione synthesis and acts as a substitute thiol. It is most effective when started early, before hepatic injury is established.

questions.stem: A man is found with a respiratory rate of 6 per minute, pinpoint pupils and reduced consciousness. Which antidote is indicated?

distractorRationale.d: This is for salicylates and some other poisons.

questions.explanation: The triad of coma, miosis and respiratory depression indicates opioid toxicity. Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist.

questions.stem: A methadone overdose patient wakes after naloxone but 2 hours later becomes drowsy with a respiratory rate of 8. What is the explanation?

options.text: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than methadone
The patient has developed an allergy to naloxone

questions.correctOptionText: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than methadone

distractorRationale.b: Allergy would not explain the pattern.

questions.explanation: Naloxone's effect lasts about 30 to 90 minutes whereas methadone lasts much longer. Observation and repeat dosing or an infusion are required.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old has tinnitus, vomiting, sweating and rapid deep breathing. Blood gases show a respiratory alkalosis with a metabolic acidosis. Which poison is most likely?

distractorRationale.d: Paracetamol does not cause this early picture.

questions.explanation: Salicylates stimulate the respiratory centre, giving respiratory alkalosis, and uncouple oxidative phosphorylation, giving metabolic acidosis. Tinnitus and sweating are typical.

questions.stem: Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in patients who are dependent on benzodiazepines or who have co-ingested pro-convulsant drugs.
questions.explanation: Reversal of benzodiazepine effect removes protection against seizures in dependent patients or those with tricyclic overdose. Supportive care is usually preferred.

questions.stem: A 75 kg adult took 30 tablets of 500 mg paracetamol. Calculate the ingested dose in mg/kg.
questions.explanation: The total is 30 x 500 = 15 000 mg, and 15 000 divided by 75 is 200 mg/kg. This should be discussed with the toxicology service.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected salicylate poisoning has Na 141, Cl 104 and bicarbonate 11 mmol/L. Calculate the anion gap in mmol/L.
questions.explanation: The sum of chloride and bicarbonate is 115, and 141 minus 115 is 26 mmol/L. This is a raised anion gap.

questions.stem: Match naloxone and flumazenil to the overdoses they treat and explain the main cautions for each. Include the case of a long-acting opioid.
markingGuide: Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity by competitive antagonism
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines at GABA-A receptors
Naloxone has a short duration and long-acting opioids such as methadone cause re-sedation
Observe and give repeat doses or an infusion
Naloxone can precipitate withdrawal in dependent patients so titrate
Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in dependence or with pro-convulsant co-ingestants
Supportive airway care is often the mainstay for benzodiazepines
questions.explanation: Both antidotes are competitive antagonists with shorter action than many agents. Marking should reward the cautions linked to dependence and duration.

questions.stem: Describe the pathophysiology and clinical features of salicylate poisoning and outline its management.
markingGuide: Respiratory centre stimulation giving hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis
Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation giving heat, raised metabolism, lactate and metabolic acidosis
Features: tinnitus, vomiting, sweating, fever, agitation or confusion
Severe: seizures, coma and pulmonary oedema
Charcoal if recent, fluids, potassium and intravenous bicarbonate for urinary alkalinisation
questions.explanation: Features follow from two mechanisms: respiratory stimulation and metabolic uncoupling. Marking should reward linking mechanism to features and treatment.
